Article Title: Anthropic allows managers to monitor employees’ Claude usage; company says: It will report on ...
Article Text:
“Smart reports analyze how a team uses Claude and report on the work getting done, what it costs at list price, where sessions run into friction, and which repeated patterns are worth packaging as shared skills,”

Who can enable the feature

What can managers see in Smart Reports

Team reports can identify individual employees

Privacy restrictions mentioned by Anthropic

Anthropic is giving managers more visibility into workplace Claude usage. Its Smart Reports feature analyses samples of team conversations, groups them by the work performed and shows associated costs. Available on Claude Enterprise plans, the tool can cover chat, Claude Code and Claude Cowork, depending on an organisation’s configuration.Anthropic wrote in a blog post.The feature is disabled by default and requires an organisation owner to enable it. Names are hidden initially, but organisations can separately permit authorised viewers to reveal users’ identities. Anthropic says organisations should not use the reports to evaluate individual performance or make employment decisions.Each eligible organisation can generate up to 10 reports monthly at no charge. Reports usually take a few hours to produce. Smart Reports are unavailable to Enterprise organizations using customer-managed encryption keys, a HIPAA configuration or certain hybrid deployments.Where zero data retention is enabled for Claude Code, reports exclude Claude Code and cover chat and Cowork instead.Authorised users can select a team, products and a reporting period covering up to the previous 28 days. They can also choose focus areas and add questions for Claude to answer while analysing transcripts.Claude reads a sample of conversations and groups sessions into workstreams and output types, such as analysis, documentation, content drafts and code. Reports show spending at list prices, average costs by output type and obstacles encountered during tasks.Viewers can open a workstream to see sessions ranked by cost. Each eligible session includes a paragraph-long summary, the product used, the date and the output type.Reports also identify recurring problems, including tool failures, missing integrations, sign-in restrictions and repeated attempts to correct unsuitable output. Recommendations can highlight workflows worth turning into shared skills.Anthropic provides a separate “Allow attribution to individual users” setting, which is also off by default. When attribution is disabled, session details display “User” instead of a name and hide session identifiers. If the organisation enables attribution, viewers still see anonymous labels initially but can use a control to reveal names and session identifiers. Each reveal is logged.This means the feature does not guarantee anonymity across every configuration. Access depends on organisational settings, permissions and how a report is shared. Owners and administrators with analytics access can create reports. Organisations can also give team leads or department heads access limited to assigned groups.The documentation lists mandatory safeguards for sensitive subjects, including health, protected characteristics, union activity, harassment complaints, whistleblowing, political or religious views and personal matters.Custom questions about restricted topics are blocked. Sessions Claude identifies as involving those topics are included only in aggregate analysis, without session summaries. Personal conversations also exclude individual session details and names.These protections depend on Claude identifying the relevant content. The documentation describes the safeguards but does not establish how reliably that classification works in practice.
Article Summary: Anthropic is giving managers more visibility into workplace Claude usage. Smart Reports analyses samples of team conversations, groups them by the work performed and shows associated costs. Available on Claude Enterprise plans, the tool can cover chat, Claude Code and Claude Cowork, depending on an organisation’s configuration.

Hugging Face CEO Clement Delangue has sent a warning to artificial intelligence (AI) CEOs. Speaking at the WIRED World Fair in Miami, he argued that while leading industry executives frequently warn about AI risks, real safety requires accountability and open development rather than corporate secrecy. He added that the biggest dangers surrounding AI will not come from open-source collaboration, but from a handful of tech giants developing frontier models in secret.“Most of the risk is actually created by a couple of players building behind closed doors. Most of the mitigation of this risk will be the full ecosystem, meaning everyone being able to build in the open,” Delangue was quoted as saying. Delangue’s warnings come from firsthand experience. Hugging Face became one of the first known companies to be struck by rogue artificial intelligence.In July, autonomous agents undergoing testing at OpenAI broke free of their testing sandbox and launched a targeted cyberattack against Hugging Face. The rogue agents went on the internet to infiltrate the startup’s systems in an effort to extract answers to evaluation tasks they had been assigned to solve. To defend its platform, Hugging Face turned to an open-weight Chinese model called GLM-5.2 to investigate the intrusion and repel the hacking.Anthropic has also disclosed multiple instances of an AI model hacking external systems during testing.Delangue pointed out that autonomous agent misbehaviour seen so far has originated from dominant players experimenting with frontier systems behind closed doors. He cautioned that upcoming high-stakes threats, such as dangerous biological capabilities or autonomous models improving themselves recursively, are likely to emerge from these same proprietary labs.While Hugging Face decided against pursuing legal action against OpenAI following the July incident, Delangue insisted that companies deploying autonomous software must face legal consequences for what their systems do.“Cyber-attacks are illegal, and I think it’s really important we make sure that agentic cyberattacks [are] illegal. We don’t want to create an environment where there’s no ownership, there’s no responsibility for cyber-attack,” Delangue said.Despite these emerging security issues, Delangue rejected the apocalyptic narratives shared by some industry figures who claim AI presents an existential risk to human survival. Delangue stated that his “P(doom)”, which is the estimated mathematical probability of AI destroying humanity, is “close to zero,” remarking that “there are many other topics that could destroy the world.”Delangue stressed that the continued health of open-source artificial intelligence is critical to keeping power from consolidating into a tiny corporate monopoly.
